chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Financial Markets Matter to Your Job

lessons.title: The Indian Market Map: RBI, SEBI, NSE, BSE and Who Regulates What

children.text: You now know what markets do and how money travels through them. This lesson answers the question that follows: who is in charge, and who do you go to when something goes wrong. Most people in India can name RBI and SEBI but cannot say which one handles their problem. That confusion costs time in exactly the moments when time matters.

body.text: There is no single regulator of Indian finance. Responsibility is split by product, not by institution. Get the product right and the correct regulator, portal and complaint route follow automatically.

children.text: The Four Regulators You Actually Deal With

body.caption: Who Regulates What in Indian Finance
headers: Where It Touches You or Your Company

cells: RBI
Banks, NBFCs, payment systems, the rupee, monetary policy, government borrowing
Salary account, company loans and limits, UPI, the repo rate that moves your EMI
SEBI
Stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, listed company disclosures, IPOs, commodity and currency derivatives on exchanges
Demat account, SIPs, your employer's quarterly results, the insider trading code you sign
IRDAI
Insurance companies, insurance products and agents
Term plan, motor policy, the group health cover your employer buys
PFRDA
The National Pension System and its intermediaries
Your NPS account, and the corporate NPS benefit if your employer offers one
EPFO (under the Labour Ministry)
The Employees' Provident Fund and related schemes
The EPF deduction on every salary slip
MCA and IBBI
Company law, filings and the insolvency process
Incorporation, annual filings, and what happens if a customer goes bankrupt

body.text: A simple rule of thumb: if the money sits with a bank or moves as payment, think RBI. If the money is invested in securities, think SEBI. If it is a policy with a claim, think IRDAI. If it is retirement money, think PFRDA or EPFO.

body.title: RBI vs SEBI: The Two That Get Confused Most

columns.label: RBI, the Central Bank
points: Set up under the RBI Act, 1934
Sets the repo rate and manages inflation and liquidity
Licenses and supervises banks and NBFCs
Manages the rupee and the government's borrowing programme
Its decisions change what borrowing costs and what deposits earn

columns.label: SEBI, the Markets Regulator
points: Given statutory powers under the SEBI Act, 1992
Protects investors and polices market conduct
Registers brokers, mutual funds, research analysts and merchant bankers
Sets disclosure rules for listed companies, including insider trading norms
Its decisions change what companies must tell you and how markets behave

body.title: Whose Desk Is This?
body.question: Your company's treasury team wants to park ₹12 crore in a liquid mutual fund, and separately wants to renegotiate its cash credit limit with the bank. Which regulator governs which part?
options: SEBI governs both, since money is being invested
RBI governs both, since a bank is involved
SEBI governs the mutual fund, RBI governs the bank limit
Neither, since corporate treasury activity is unregulated
body.explanation: Mutual funds are securities products, registered with and regulated by SEBI. A cash credit limit is bank lending, governed by RBI rules on lending, exposure and provisioning. The same company, on the same day, deals with two different regulators depending on the product.

children.text: Almost every rule you now take for granted, dematerialised shares, fast settlement, a statutory regulator, exists because something went badly wrong first. The sequence is worth knowing, because it explains why Indian markets are structured the way they are.

body.title: The Indian Market, in Eight Steps

events.title: BSE Is Founded
events.description: Brokers trading under a banyan tree in Mumbai formalise into what becomes the Bombay Stock Exchange, the oldest stock exchange in Asia.

events.title: SEBI Is Created
events.description: SEBI is set up as an administrative body, initially without statutory teeth, to bring order to a fragmented and often opaque market.

events.title: The Harshad Mehta Scam and the SEBI Act
events.description: A large scam exploiting gaps between the banking and securities systems breaks. SEBI is given statutory powers under the SEBI Act, 1992, and the modern regulatory era begins.

events.title: NSE Begins Trading
events.description: NSE launches screen-based, anonymous electronic trading, ending the open outcry floor and the information advantage brokers held over ordinary investors.

events.title: Demat Arrives With NSDL
events.description: NSDL is set up and shares begin moving from paper certificates to electronic form. CDSL follows in 1999. Forged certificates and lost share paperwork largely disappear.

events.title: Rolling Settlement Tightens to T+2
events.description: Trades settle two working days after the trade, replacing slower and riskier cycles, and carry-forward practices like badla are gone.

events.title: Commodity Regulation Moves to SEBI
events.description: The Forward Markets Commission is merged into SEBI, bringing commodity derivatives under the same regulator as equities.

events.title: T+1 Settlement Completed
events.description: India completes the phased move to T+1 settlement, becoming one of the first major markets to do so. An optional shorter cycle has since been introduced in beta for a limited set of stocks.

stats.label: NSE Electronic Trading
stats.context: Screen-based and anonymous from day one

stats.label: Settlement Cycle Today
stats.context: Money and shares settle one working day after the trade

children.text: NSE and BSE: Two Exchanges, One Price

markDefs.definition: A marketplace that lists securities and matches buy and sell orders between members, under rules approved by the regulator.
Buying an asset in one market and simultaneously selling it in another to profit from a price difference. Arbitrage activity is what keeps the same share priced almost identically on NSE and BSE.

children.text: Most large Indian companies are listed on both exchanges, so the same share trades on NSE and on BSE at the same time. Each
runs its own order book, yet the two prices stay within paise of each other, because traders practising
instantly buy on the cheaper venue and sell on the dearer one until the gap closes.

body.label: Same Company, Two Tickers
body.context: Reliance on NSE and Reliance on BSE are the same shares in the same demat account. Where you bought does not change what you own.

body.title: Who Actually Guarantees That Your Trade Settles?

children.text: When you buy shares, you never meet the seller and have no way to judge whether they will deliver. Three institutions make that irrelevant:
matches your order with an anonymous counterparty, on price and time priority, so no one gets preferential treatment.

steps in between the two sides, becoming buyer to the seller and seller to the buyer. It collects margins upfront and maintains a settlement guarantee fund, so if your counterparty defaults, you still get your shares.
NSDL or CDSL holds the shares electronically in your name and moves them between accounts on settlement day.

This is why your shares sit with the depository rather than with your broker, and why a broker going out of business does not, by itself, take your holdings with it. Check the consolidated account statement that NSDL or CDSL sends you directly, not just your broker's app.
When Something Goes Wrong: Where to Complain

body.caption: Match the Problem to the Right Door

cells: Broker will not transfer your funds, or a mutual fund issue is unresolved
SEBI SCORES portal, after first complaining to the intermediary
SEBI
Bank fee dispute, failed UPI transfer, loan account error
The bank's grievance channel, then the RBI ombudsman scheme
RBI
Insurance claim rejected or delayed
The insurer's grievance cell, then the IRDAI grievance portal or the Insurance Ombudsman
IRDAI
NPS contribution not credited or wrongly allocated
Your NPS service provider, then the PFRDA grievance mechanism
PFRDA
EPF withdrawal stuck or employer not depositing PF
The EPFO grievance portal
EPFO
Someone promising guaranteed returns on shares
Check registration first, then report to SEBI
SEBI

body.text: Almost every regulator expects you to complain to the institution first and give it a defined window to respond, before escalating. Skipping that step usually gets your complaint sent straight back. Keep the reference number the institution gives you, because the escalation portal will ask for it.

body.label: SEBI SCORES: Investor Grievance Portal
body.description: SEBI's complaint portal for issues with brokers, mutual funds, listed companies and other registered intermediaries. Worth bookmarking before you need it.

body.title: The WhatsApp Group With Guaranteed Returns
body.scenario: A colleague at your Hyderabad office forwards you a WhatsApp group where an "advisor" shares daily stock tips and promises 4% monthly returns. He asks members to transfer money to a personal account so the advisor can trade on their behalf. Two people on your team have already sent ₹2 lakh each, and one is asking you whether to send more.
body.prompt: What do you check, and what do you tell them?
body.modelAnswer: Start with three checks. First, registration: search SEBI's list of registered intermediaries for the person or firm, since anyone giving investment advice for a fee must be a SEBI-registered investment adviser or research analyst. Second, the money trail: a legitimate arrangement never requires you to transfer funds to an individual's personal account, because your money should move from your own bank account to your own broking or demat account, which stays in your name. Third, the promise itself: 4% a month compounds to roughly 60% a year, and no one can guarantee that; a guaranteed return on equity is a contradiction and is itself a red flag SEBI repeatedly warns about. Tell your colleagues to stop sending money immediately, keep every message, receipt and transfer record, complain in writing to their bank about the transfers, and report the matter on SEBI SCORES and to the cyber crime portal. Do not let anyone send more money on the promise of recovering what is already lost, because that is the standard second stage of these frauds.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: An unresolved complaint against a stockbroker or mutual fund is escalated on SEBI's ___ portal.
body.explanation: SCORES is SEBI's centralised investor grievance system. Complain to the intermediary first, keep the reference number, and escalate on SCORES if it is not resolved within the stated timeline.

body.title: Before You or Your Company Hands Money to Anyone
steps: Confirm the entity is registered with the relevant regulator, and match the registration number against the regulator's own website rather than a screenshot
Confirm that money moves only between accounts in your own name, never to an individual's personal account
Read what is guaranteed and what is not, remembering that market-linked returns can never be guaranteed
Save the grievance escalation route for that product before you invest, not after a problem appears
For anything your employer offers, ask HR which regulator governs it, because EPF, NPS, insurance and ESOPs sit with four different ones

cards.definition: Reserve Bank of India. The central bank: monetary policy, banks, NBFCs, payments and the rupee.
Securities and Exchange Board of India. The securities market regulator, with statutory powers since the SEBI Act, 1992.
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. Regulates insurers, insurance products and agents.
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority. Regulates the National Pension System and its intermediaries.
The two depositories that hold shares in electronic form and move them between demat accounts on settlement.
The institution that stands between buyer and seller, collects margins and guarantees that trades settle even if a counterparty defaults.
Shares and money change hands one working day after the trade date, the cycle Indian equity markets moved to fully in 2023.

body.title: One Last Sorting Test
body.question: Your employer is listed, and it delays disclosing a large order win to the exchanges while a few senior employees buy shares. Which regulator has jurisdiction over that conduct?
options: RBI, because bank accounts were used to buy the shares
SEBI, because it covers listed company disclosure and insider trading
MCA, because it is a company law matter
The stock exchange alone, since the shares trade there
body.explanation: Disclosure obligations of listed companies and insider trading both sit squarely with SEBI. Exchanges do have their own surveillance and will flag unusual activity, but enforcement powers here belong to SEBI. Chapter 6 covers what this means for you personally as an employee of a listed company.

points: Indian finance is regulated by product, not by institution: RBI for banking, payments and the rupee, SEBI for securities markets, IRDAI for insurance, PFRDA and EPFO for retirement money
SEBI became a statutory regulator through the SEBI Act, 1992, after the Harshad Mehta scam exposed the gaps between banking and securities
Electronic trading on NSE from 1994, demat from 1996 and faster settlement cycles turned a paper-based market into one of the fastest-settling markets in the world
The same share trades on both NSE and BSE at nearly identical prices, because arbitrage closes any gap almost instantly
Clearing corporations guarantee settlement and depositories hold your shares, which is why your holdings do not depend on your broker staying in business

Complain to the institution first and keep the reference number, then escalate to the right portal: SCORES for securities, the ombudsman route for banking, and the equivalent for insurance and pensions

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal, investment or financial advice. Regulatory structures, portals and settlement cycles change over time, so confirm current requirements on the relevant regulator's own website before acting.
